source: MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension (នាយកដ្ឋានផ្សព្វផ្សាយកសិកម្ម), "បច្ចេកទេសដាំដុះសណ្តែកបាយ" (Mung Bean Cultivation Techniques handbook), Kingdom of Cambodia, MAFF, published by the Department of Agricultural Extension. Reference list on the closing page cites additional 2003-dated MAFF/agricultural-extension source booklets on mung bean varieties, seed production, and pest management, plus several international references (Plant Resources of South-East Asia Vol. I, 1992; Talekar & Skinner, Field Guide to Insect Pests of Tropical Asia, 1995; Nelson, Insect Pests of Vegetables, Philippines, 1969; Mung Bean Adaptation Trial, Kbalkoh Station 1996-2000, CLV Network; and a 1991 Bangkok workshop proceedings on Yellow Mosaic Virus). No elibrary.maff.gov.kh URL is visible on the scanned pages provided, so none is given here. Uploaded as a 38-page scanned PDF; no embedded text layer, all content read visually from page images. text: Black cutworm (ដង្កូវកាត់ដើម, Agrotis ipsilon, family Noctuidae, order Lepidoptera) moths lay eggs on leaf surfaces or plant debris; eggs hatch in about 2 days. Larvae are active/hide during the day depending on temperature and food availability and can complete their life cycle over roughly 2 weeks to 5 months; pupation in the soil lasts roughly 1-4 weeks. Larvae damage mung bean by cutting through seedling stems at or near the soil line during germination and early growth, killing young plants. Prevention: inspect soil/field before planting and remove crop residue that harbors larvae and pupae; keep the sowing area free of debris that shelters eggs and larvae. Control: active ingredients named include Acephate, Chlorantraniliprole, Cypermethrin, Emamectin benzoate, Fipronil, Flubendiamide, Permethrin, and Indoxacarb.
